wuduSteps.title: Set your intention
wuduSteps.body: In your heart, intend that this wudu is so you can pray. There is no formula to say out loud.

wuduSteps.title: Begin with Allah's name
wuduSteps.body: Say Bismillah if you remember. If you forget, carry on. There is no need to start again.

wuduSteps.title: Wash hands
wuduSteps.body: Wash both hands up to the wrists, making sure water reaches between the fingers.

wuduSteps.title: Rinse mouth and nose
wuduSteps.body: Rinse your mouth, then gently clean your nose. Use as much water as is comfortable and safe.

wuduSteps.title: Wash face
wuduSteps.body: Wash the face from the hairline to the chin and from ear to ear.

wuduSteps.title: Wash arms
wuduSteps.body: Wash the right arm through the elbow, then the left arm through the elbow.

wuduSteps.title: Wipe head and ears
wuduSteps.body: With wet hands, wipe over your head. Most beginner guides also have you wipe your ears once.

wuduSteps.title: Wash feet
wuduSteps.body: Wash the right foot through the ankle, then the left foot through the ankle.

ghuslSteps.title: Set your intention
ghuslSteps.body: In your heart, intend a full-body wash for the sake of Allah. The minimum is that water reaches your whole body, including the roots of your hair.

ghuslSteps.title: Wash private areas if needed
ghuslSteps.body: Clean whatever needs cleaning first, privately, before you go on.

ghuslSteps.title: Make wudu
ghuslSteps.body: Make wudu as part of the ghusl. If your wudu breaks afterwards, do it again before you pray.

ghuslSteps.title: Wash head and hair roots
ghuslSteps.body: Get the water down to your scalp and hair roots as best you can. If you have braids, a medical dressing, or hair that makes this hard, ask someone qualified.

ghuslSteps.title: Wash the whole body
ghuslSteps.body: Wash your whole body so water reaches the skin everywhere, usually the right side first and then the left.

wuduBreaks: Using the toilet: passing urine or stool, and passing wind. A hadith says prayer is not accepted from someone whose wudu has broken until they make wudu again.
Deep sleep. The schools differ on details, such as sleeping while sitting firmly.
Losing consciousness. Scholars treat this like sleep.
If you only think you passed wind, your wudu stands until you are sure, for example when you hear a sound or notice a smell.
ghuslNeeded: After sexual intimacy or a sexual discharge, including a wet dream.
After menstruation or bleeding after childbirth ends.
On becoming Muslim. The schools differ on whether this is required or recommended. See the note below.

commonCorrections.title: I keep restarting because I feel unsure.
commonCorrections.body: Do the steps once, with attention, then stop. Repeating out of anxiety turns purification into something that wears you down.

commonCorrections.title: I forgot one recommended detail.
commonCorrections.body: Nothing has gone wrong. Learn the essentials first, then ask a teacher which parts are required in your school of law.

commonCorrections.title: Water is hard to use because of illness or injury.
commonCorrections.body: Ask a qualified person about the concessions, such as wiping over a bandage, or tayammum. Islam does not ask you to make your health worse.

commonCorrections.title: I am confused by different videos.
commonCorrections.body: Pick one reliable beginner method and learn it properly. Small differences between teachers do not mean your worship is broken.

wuduVideo.note: This video has background music at the start and no spoken English. It shows one method; small details differ between schools.

ghuslVideo.title: How to make ghusl, the full-body wash
ghuslVideo.note: Shows a simple way and the fuller Sunnah way. Schools differ on whether rinsing the mouth and nose is required in ghusl.

wuduBreaksDiffer: Bleeding and vomiting. In the Hanafi school, a mouthful of vomit breaks wudu, and so does blood from the mouth that equals or outweighs the saliva. Other teaching, such as the Islamic Foundation of Ireland booklet, says bleeding and vomiting do not break it.
Touching your private parts directly. Some teaching lists it as breaking wudu (the Ireland booklet does). It is not on the Hanafi list.
Laughing out loud in prayer. The Hanafi list includes an adult laughing out loud during a prayer with bowing and prostration. The Ireland booklet lists laughing in prayer as not breaking wudu.
wuduBreaksNote: No single source we checked compares all four schools side by side. If one of these comes up often for you, ask a local teacher which view you follow.

wuduBreaksImage.alt: Two boxes. The first, what breaks wudu for everyone: using the toilet, passing wind, deep sleep and losing consciousness. The second, points where the schools differ: bleeding, vomiting and touching the private parts. A note says a doubt alone does not break wudu.
wuduBreaksImage.caption: What breaks wudu, and where the schools differ.

points: Your Shahada is valid without it. The wash is not a condition of becoming Muslim.
A hadith reports the Prophet telling a man who had just become Muslim to bathe (Sunan Abi Dawud 355, graded Sahih by al-Albani).
In the relied-upon Hanafi and Shafi'i view, the wash is recommended, and it is required if you were already in a state that needs ghusl, such as after sexual intimacy.
The Maliki and Hanbali schools are reported to treat it as required in all cases, though the sources we checked disagree on the Hanbali position.
If you have not done it yet, do it when you can, and before you pray if you were in a state that needs ghusl. A local imam can help you with your own situation.

wuduImage.alt: Eight faceless panels showing wudu in order: intention, hands, mouth and nose, face, arms to the elbows, wiping the head, ears, and feet to the ankles.
wuduImage.caption: Wudu in order. Washing each part once is the minimum, and three times is the Sunnah.

ghuslImage.alt: Five simple panels showing ghusl: intention, washing the hands and private parts, wudu, water over the head to the hair roots, then the whole body.
ghuslImage.caption: Ghusl, the full-body wash, in five steps.

tayammum.summary: When you cannot use water, because there is none, or because you are ill or injured and water would harm you, there is a dry alternative called tayammum. The Quran allows it for people who are ill, travelling or cannot find water.
steps: Make the intention in your heart and say Bismillah.
Lightly strike clean earth, or a natural surface with dust on it, with both palms.
Blow or shake off the excess, then wipe your face.
tayammum.schoolNote: One method uses a single strike and wipes the hands to the wrists, as in Sahih al-Bukhari 338. The Hanafi method uses two strikes: one for the face, and a second to wipe both arms including the elbows.
tayammum.ends: Tayammum ends when you find water you can use, and with anything that breaks wudu or calls for ghusl.
tayammum.referral: If an illness or injury keeps you away from water for a while, ask a local teacher how to manage it day to day.

video.title: How to make tayammum

commonQuestions.question: In winter, can I wipe over my socks instead of washing my feet?
commonQuestions.answer: Many scholars allow wiping over leather footwear (khuffs) or suitable socks, with conditions. You must have put them on after a full wudu, and the permission lasts one day and night at home, or three days and nights when travelling. For ghusl you still wash your feet. The schools differ on which socks count. In the Hanafi answer we link, they must be sturdy enough to walk about 3.5 miles (5.5 km) in without tearing, and water must not soak through, so ordinary dress socks usually do not qualify while hiking socks often do. Other teaching allows ordinary socks. Ask your local imam which view your community follows.

commonQuestions.question: Can I make wudu while wearing nail polish?
commonQuestions.answer: Regular nail polish stops water reaching your nails, so wudu made over it does not count. If you made wudu first and then put the polish on, you can pray with that wudu. Take the polish off before your next wudu. If you are unsure about a particular product, ask a local teacher.

commonQuestions.question: I have a cast or a bandage. How do I make wudu?
commonQuestions.answer: The Hanafi answer we link says: wash the injured part if you can; if you cannot, wipe it with a wet hand; if that would harm you, wipe over most of the bandage; and if even that would cause harm, leave that part out. The Shafi'i school also wipes over the cast but adds tayammum for that limb, and in some cases the prayer is repeated later. Past experience, clear signs or a trustworthy doctor's advice help you judge harm. Please ask a local imam about your own situation.

commonQuestions.question: I wear a headscarf. Do I have to take it off to wipe my head at work?
commonQuestions.answer: In the Hanafi answer we link, you must wipe at least a quarter of the head itself, and wiping over the scarf does not count. One practical way is to loosen the front of the scarf in a private stall and slide a wet hand underneath. The Hanbali school allows wiping over a scarf that is wrapped under the chin, as long as you put it on while in wudu, for one day and night (three when travelling). A SeekersGuidance answer says you may follow the Hanbali view for this, provided your wudu and your prayer are both valid in that school. Making wudu at home and keeping it, and wiping over suitable socks for your feet, also cut down on washing at work. Ask your teacher which option suits you.

commonQuestions.question: How often should I trim my nails and remove body hair?
commonQuestions.answer: A hadith in Sahih Muslim (258) says trimming the moustache, cutting the nails and removing underarm and pubic hair should not be left for more than forty nights. A weekly grooming day, often Friday, keeps you well inside that. The modesty topic covers these grooming habits (fitrah) and the school differences on the beard.

moreCards.title: Clean clothes and a clean place (najasah)
moreCards.summary: Your body, your clothes and the spot you pray on should be free of impurity such as urine, stool or blood. Wash it until the substance, its colour and its smell are gone as far as you reasonably can.
points: A doubt does not make something impure. What you know to be clean stays clean until you are sure it is not.
Pets, a baby's wet clothes, alcohol in perfume and laundry done by family all have calm answers on the purification topic.
If you are unsure, go with what you know for certain and ask a teacher afterwards rather than skipping a prayer.

links.label: Clean clothes and a clean place

moreCards.title: If a health condition keeps breaking your wudu
moreCards.summary: Some conditions keep breaking wudu: constant wind with IBS, leaking urine, bleeding outside the period, or a stoma or catheter. Keep praying. A woman whose bleeding would not stop was told to keep praying and to make wudu for every prayer (Sahih al-Bukhari 228).
points: In the Hanafi answer we link, you count as an excused person when the condition does not leave you enough time within a prayer window to make wudu and pray the obligatory prayer without it happening.
Once you are excused, make wudu after the prayer time begins. The condition does not break that wudu until the prayer time ends, even while it carries on.
If you are not excused, a doubt still does not break your wudu. The Prophet said not to leave the prayer unless you hear a sound or notice a smell (Sahih al-Bukhari 137).
In hospital, pray in the way your body allows, sitting or lying down if you need to, and use tayammum if water would harm you. You can ask the nurses whether the hospital has a spiritual care team.
If you use a stoma bag or a catheter, ask a local imam how these rules apply to you, and keep praying while you wait for an answer.
differences: The rule above is the Hanafi one. The other schools set out the excused person differently, and we have not yet checked their own sources, so ask your teacher.
moreCards.referral: Describe your pattern to an imam once and get a clear answer for your situation. You are not being asked to make wudu again every few minutes.

istinja.title: Before wudu: cleaning after the toilet (istinja)
istinja.summary: Few people explain this, and it is awkward to ask in person. Muslims clean the private parts after using the toilet, and this cleaning (istinja) is its own step, separate from wudu. The Prophet (peace be upon him) used water for it (Sahih al-Bukhari 150), and a hadith treats carelessness about urine on the body as a serious matter (Sahih al-Bukhari 218).
points: Wipe with toilet paper first, then wash with water from a bottle, a jug or a bidet spray if you can.
Use your left hand for cleaning. The Prophet taught not to clean with the right hand (Sahih Muslim 262a).

If only paper is available, wipe until you are clean. In the Hanafi answers we link, paper alone meets the basic sunnah while the mess stays at the exit. Once it has spread beyond the exit and the area right around it, washing with water is required.
Pat dry with paper. If a spot got onto your underwear, rinse it or change before you pray.
Many Canadian washrooms have no bidet. A small refillable bottle in your bag or at work does the job.
You do not need a shower after each visit. Clean yourself, then make wudu.

Clean once, properly, then leave it. A Hanafi answer on misgivings says doubts after a proper istinja should be ignored, and it points to help for obsessive doubts (OCD) for anyone who keeps getting pulled back.
differences: Facing the qibla: the hadith forbids facing the qibla while relieving yourself (Sahih Muslim 262a). The schools differ on whether this applies inside a building, so ask your teacher. Where you can, set things up so you do not face it.
When wiping alone is enough: the rule above is the Hanafi one. We have not yet checked the other schools' conditions in their own sources, so ask your teacher.
istinja.referral: If a disability or a medical device makes this hard, ask a local imam how to manage it.
